purpose: This medication helps your body make more white blood cells after chemotherapy. Chemotherapy can lower your white blood cell count, which makes it harder for your body to fight infections. This medicine helps reduce your risk of getting serious infections during your cancer treatment.
how_it_works: Your bone marrow is like a factory that makes blood cells. This medicine acts like a natural signal in your body that tells your bone marrow to produce more infection-fighting white blood cells called neutrophils. By boosting these cells, your immune system becomes stronger and better able to protect you.
common_side_effects: Bone or muscle aching and pain (especially in the lower back, hips, or legs) is the most common side effect. You may also notice redness, swelling, or mild pain at the injection site. Some people feel tired or have headaches as well.
warnings: Tell your doctor right away if you have serious side effects like severe pain in your upper left belly or left shoulder (could be a spleen problem), trouble breathing, or signs of a serious allergic reaction like rash, swelling, or dizziness. People with sickle cell disease should use this medicine with caution. Do not shake the syringe. This medicine should not be given in the 14 days before or 24 hours after chemotherapy.
typical_dosing: This medicine is given as a single injection under the skin (subcutaneous), usually once per chemotherapy cycle. It is typically given about 24 hours after your chemotherapy is finished. Your doctor or nurse will give you the injection, or they may teach you how to give it at home using an on-body injector device.
